description: Yellow diamond warning sign carrying a black elephant silhouette, posted on forested highway stretches.

image.prompt:
Product photograph of one isolated object, shot from a HIGH THREE-QUARTER ANGLE: the camera is well above the object and tilted down about 30 degrees, so the top of the object is clearly visible along with its front and one side. Not a straight-on elevation.

The object: Slim galvanised post carrying a flat square plate rotated forty-five degrees to stand as a diamond on its point, plate face bright yellow with a black border band following the diamond edge and a solid black elephant silhouette filling the centre, a smaller rectangular yellow supplementary plate mounted on the post directly below carrying black lettering reading the Thai line ระวังช้าง above a smaller roman line reading ELEPHANT CROSSING Materials: Bright yellow retroreflective sheeting gone chalky and slightly greened at the edges, solid black pictogram paint, galvanised post with rust at the ground line, insect and road spatter across the lower face.

Legend: this object is a SIGN, and its printed legend is part of the object, not an annotation on the photograph. Render every letter, numeral, pictogram, arrow and coloured band described above, exactly as described and nothing more. Thai script must be rendered as Thai script with correct glyph shapes, above the roman line where both are described. Lettering and pictograms lie flat on the sign face, sharp, high-contrast and correctly proportioned, and the face must stay legible despite the camera angle. Do not leave the face blank, do not substitute lorem or invented wording, and do not add any text that was not described.

Form: build the object from a few simple, chunky, closed volumes. Prefer solid panels over lattice, mesh, grilles or perforated screens; keep any openings few, large and clearly separated. No thin spindly protrusions, no wires, no chains, no fringes, no lace, no fine filigree, no dense repeated slots or cut-outs. Keep the silhouette simple and readable from every side. Keep the object's SHAPE simple; richness must come from the surface finish, wear and materials rather than from intricate geometry. The object is still photoreal and highly detailed in its texture -- only its form is simple.

Framing: long-lens near-orthographic perspective, minimal foreshortening. The object is perfectly centred and occupies about 75% of the frame height, with clear empty margin on all four sides. The whole object is in frame; nothing is cropped.

Background: completely flat seamless neutral 50% grey (#808080). The object floats in empty space against an infinite seamless backdrop, photographed as a cut-out with nothing underneath it. There is no surface for it to rest on and nothing for it to cast a shadow onto. No floor, no ground plane, no horizon line, no cast shadow, no contact shadow, no reflection, no vignette, no gradient.

Lighting: flat even studio illumination from all sides, soft and shadowless, like a lightbox. No strong key light, no rim light, no coloured light, no specular blowout, no dramatic highlights. Colours must read as true albedo.

One object only, nothing else in frame. No people, no hands, no other props, no packaging, no watermarks, no drop shadow, and no border around the photograph itself.

Photoreal, sharp focus edge to edge, clean and undamaged geometry, realistic materials and surface wear. Not stylised, not cartoon, not low-poly, not a 3D render preview, not a wireframe.

license.notice: Fully synthetic. No third-party scanned or scraped geometry.

review.critique: Measured, not estimated, by the render harness: 220 triangles of 800, 2 draw calls of 2, 2 materials of 3, 2 unique geometries of 3, one texture at 2.7 MB, and createObjectModel returning in 34 ms. DRAW CALLS are the binding axis and triangles are not - the prop sits at a quarter of its triangle budget and at 100% of its draw-call budget - and that is the design rather than an overrun, because it was decided in the BLOCKOUT and not optimised into at the end. Three splits were refused and each is recorded where someone tempted to make it will read it: the supplementary plate folds into the diamond's buffer, the plate faces do NOT get a graphic material separate from their backs, and the fasteners stay printed. The UV atlas is what makes the second of those possible - front-facing vertices take a graphic region and every other vertex collapses to a single galvanised texel, so one material carries a printed front and a plain back. NOTHING WAS DECIMATED and no segment count was cut: at 220 triangles the vertex cost is already below the per-draw-call overhead, so a decimated LOD tier would save nothing measurable and would cost a second geometry against a ceiling of three. The one place triangles WERE spent is the post's 8 height segments, 56 of them, to carry a weathering ramp that would otherwise have needed a texture. The factory was regenerated at this pass id and the post-generation layer re-applied through a recorded script, so the shipped artefact is the generator's own output plus a layer whose every part is described in the spec.

featureReviews.evidence: Unchanged by optimisation: nothing was decimated and no segment count was reduced. 220 triangles measured in the harness against a budget of 800.
Costs zero triangles and zero draw calls - it is texels in an atlas that is built once at module scope and shared by every instance of the prop.
Same atlas, same zero marginal cost. 1024x512 at 2.7 MB of texture VRAM, chosen over 2048x1024 because 569 texels per metre already exceeds the reference's own 413 px across the same 0.90 m.

Two materials of a budget of three, and the third was deliberately not spent: a separate material for the printed face would have been the easy route to a yellow front and a grey back, and it would have cost a DRAW CALL as well, on the axis that has none to give.
Two unique geometries of a budget of three. Both are shared across every instance.

The post's rust ramp costs 56 triangles - the box is rebuilt at 8 height segments instead of 1, because two rows of vertices can only carry a linear ramp from top to bottom, which would rust the whole post. Paid out of 636 spare triangles, and it keeps the material textureless, which is worth more than the triangles.

name: Elephant Crossing Sign
nameTh: ป้ายระวังช้าง
notes: The diamond-on-point plate is the warning sign proper and the elephant pictogram is a solid filled silhouette rather than an outline, which is what lets it read at highway distance and survive a low texture resolution. The small rectangular supplementary plate below carrying the wording is how these are actually posted on Thai highways, and it is part of this asset rather than a separate prop because the two are always mounted on one post. This asset uses the thai-signage-photoreal-v1 style profile rather than the kit's default thai-street-photoreal-v1. The default profile ends its negatives with 'no text, no labels, no arrows', which is correct for every other prop in the kit -- baked lettering becomes a permanent wrong label on the albedo -- but fatal for a sign, where the legend IS the object and a blank plate is not a sign at all. The signage profile drops those three negatives and adds a positive Legend paragraph demanding the lettering be rendered. Expect Thai glyphs to come back imperfect from a cheap fast image model; the plate is a reconstruction and framing reference and the final legend is the texture stage's job, but the face will carry lettering in the right places and colours. Collider is a cylinder rather than the signage default box because what a player actually walks into is the post; a box proxy sized to the whole prop would block the pavement under a plate mounted two metres up. Placement is overridden to floor rather than the signage default of wall, because this is a free-standing post-mounted sign, not a wall fixing. Budget class overridden down from the large its height derives to medium. Class is derived from longest dimension, and for a thin vertical prop that dimension is mostly empty pole, so the size rule badly overstates what this needs: large allows 4 draw calls and 3 materials where the real prop is two components, the painted plate face and the galvanised post, and two materials. Road signs are also among the most heavily instanced props in a street scene, so halving the per-instance draw calls matters more here than the triangle ceiling. No destruction groups.
